r-pm-definition-sphere.title: Project manager defined; sphere of influence (project, organisation, industry, profession, across disciplines)
r-pm-definition-sphere.notes: Conductor analogy continued: neither leader must play every instrument/role but needs domain knowledge, and both lead, plan and coordinate through written (scores/plans) and real-time (baton/meetings, verbal and nonverbal cues) communication. Definition: the PM is the person assigned by the performing organisation to lead the team responsible for achieving project objectives - distinct from a functional manager (oversight of a functional/business unit) and an operations manager (efficient operations). Sphere of influence (Figure 3-1): project team, sponsors, governing bodies, steering committees, PMOs, portfolio/program/project managers, resource managers, other stakeholders, suppliers, customers, end users. The project: lead the team, balance competing constraints with resources, communicate between sponsor, team and stakeholders, present the vision of success, use soft skills to reach consensus (relevant stakeholders support decisions even without 100% agreement). Research: the top 2% of PMs show superior relationship and communication skills and a positive attitude. Communication practices: multiple methods; create and follow communications plans; predictable, consistent; understand needs (communication may be the only deliverable some stakeholders get until the end); concise, clear, complete, simple, relevant, tailored; include positive and negative news; feedback channels; relationship skills and networks - informal networks matter more than formal ones. The organisation: interact with other PMs (shared resources, funding priorities, deliverable hand-offs, goal alignment); advocacy role; work with sponsor on internal political/strategic issues; build PM competency; tacit and explicit knowledge transfer; demonstrate value of PM, raise acceptance, advance the PMO; may report to a functional manager, PMO, portfolio or program manager; may be an external consultant. The industry: stay informed on product/technology development, market niches, standards, support tools, economic forces, discipline influences, process improvement and sustainability. Professional discipline: contribute knowledge (communities of practice) and keep learning in PM, related and other professions. Across disciplines: act as informal ambassador for the value of PM (timeliness, quality, innovation, resource management).

r-talent-triangle.title: PMI Talent Triangle: technical project management, leadership, strategic and business management
r-talent-triangle.notes: Based on the Project Manager Competency Development (PMCD) Framework. Technical project management = knowledge, skills and behaviours for specific domains of project, program and portfolio management. Leadership = guide, motivate and direct a team to help the organisation achieve business goals. Strategic and business management = industry and organisational expertise that enhances performance and delivers business outcomes. Technical skills alone are not enough; organisations want leadership and business intelligence; PMs need a balance of all three. Top PMs: focus on critical technical elements and have key artefacts at hand (critical success factors, schedule, selected financial reports, issue log); tailor traditional and agile tools; plan thoroughly and prioritise; manage schedule, cost, resources, risks; rely on expert judgment and know where to find expertise. Strategic/business skills: see the high-level organisation, negotiate and implement decisions supporting alignment and innovation; working knowledge of finance, marketing, operations; domain knowledge; explain the business aspects of the project, develop a delivery strategy with sponsor, team and SMEs, implement it to maximise business value; consult operational managers. Be able to explain strategy, mission, goals, products/services, operations, market and competition; apply strategy, mission, goals, priority, tactics and products to the project; weigh risks and issues, financial implications, cost vs benefit (NPV, ROI), business value, benefits realisation, scope/budget/schedule/quality; keep business and project strategies aligned with the sponsor as conditions change.

r-leadership-qualities.title: Leadership skills, dealing with people and qualities of a leader
r-leadership-qualities.notes: Leadership = ability to guide, motivate and direct a team (negotiation, resilience, communication, problem solving, critical thinking, interpersonal skills). People are the common denominator - 'people can be counted, but they are not numbers'. Study behaviours and motivations; lead all stakeholders including steering team and sponsors. Qualities: visionary; optimistic; collaborative; managing relationships and conflict (trust, satisfying concerns, consensus, balancing goals, persuasion, negotiation, compromise, conflict resolution, networks, long-term view, political acumen); communicating (top PMs spend about 90% of their time communicating; manage expectations; accept feedback graciously; give it constructively; ask and listen); respectful, courteous, honest, trustworthy, loyal, ethical; integrity, cultural sensitivity, courage, problem solving, decisiveness; giving credit; life-long learner, results- and action-oriented; focusing on the important (continuous prioritisation, strategic vs tactical priorities, vigilance on primary constraints, sifting information); holistic and systemic view; critical thinking and being a change agent; building effective teams, service orientation, humour.

r-politics-power.title: Politics, power and getting things done: forms of power
r-politics-power.notes: Politics involves influence, negotiation, autonomy and power and is neither good nor bad in itself. The PM observes the project and organisational landscape, reviews data in context and selects the right kind of power to influence and negotiate, while respecting others and maintaining their autonomy. Power may stem from individual or organisational traits and is supported by others' perception. Forms: positional (formal, authoritative, legitimate), informational, referent (respect/admiration, credibility), situational (e.g., crisis), personal or charismatic, relational (networks, alliances), expert, reward-oriented, punitive or coercive, ingratiating, pressure-based, guilt-based, persuasive, avoiding. Top PMs are proactive and intentional: they acquire the power and authority they need within organisational policies rather than wait for it to be granted.

r-leadership-vs-management.title: Leadership vs management; leadership styles; personality
r-leadership-vs-management.notes: Management directs a person from one point to another using known expected behaviours; leadership works with others through discussion or debate to guide them. Table 3-1: management directs using positional power, maintains, administrates, focuses on systems and structure, relies on control, near-term goals, asks how and when, focuses on bottom line, accepts the status quo, does things right, focuses on operational issues and problem solving. Leadership guides, influences and collaborates using relational power, develops, innovates, focuses on relationships, inspires trust, long-range vision, asks what and why, focuses on the horizon, challenges the status quo, does the right things, focuses on vision, alignment, motivation, inspiration. PMs need both; the skill is the balance. Style factors: leader, team member, organisational and environmental characteristics. Styles: laissez-faire (hands-off), transactional (goals, feedback, rewards; management by exception), servant leader (serve first; others' growth, autonomy, well-being; leadership emerges after service), transformational (idealised attributes, inspirational motivation, innovation, individual consideration), charismatic, interactional (mix of transactional, transformational, charismatic). Personality traits: authentic, courteous, creative, cultural, emotional, intellectual, managerial, political, service-oriented, social, systemic; emphasis varies by situation.

r-performing-integration.title: Performing integration at process, cognitive and context levels; complexity
r-performing-integration.notes: Two-fold integration role: work with the sponsor to align project objectives with portfolio, program and business strategy; and guide the team to focus on what is essential by integrating processes, knowledge and people. Process level: processes overlap and recur (e.g., a requirement change affecting scope, schedule or budget raises a change request handled through Control Scope and Perform Integrated Change Control, which runs throughout); failing to integrate interacting processes leaves little chance of meeting objectives. Cognitive level: method depends on size, complexity and culture; PM becomes proficient in all Knowledge Areas and applies experience, insight, leadership, technical and business skills. Context level: new technologies, social networks, multicultural aspects, virtual teams and new values; consider them in communications planning and knowledge management. Complexity (Navigating Complexity practice guide) arises from system behaviour (interdependencies of components and systems), human behaviour (interplay of individuals and groups) and ambiguity (uncertainty of emerging issues, confusion). Complexity is a perception; a project 'contains' complexity. Properties: multiple parts, many connections, dynamic interactions, emergent behaviour not explained by the sum of the parts.

i-integration-overview.title: Project Integration Management: purpose, the seven processes and their ITTOs
i-integration-overview.notes: Integration = identify, define, combine, unify and coordinate processes and activities across Process Groups; characteristics of unification, consolidation, communication and interrelationship, from start to completion. Choices about resource allocation, balancing competing demands, alternative approaches, tailoring, managing interdependencies among Knowledge Areas. Processes: 4.1 Develop Project Charter (document formally authorising the project and giving the PM authority to apply resources); 4.2 Develop Project Management Plan (define, prepare, coordinate all components and consolidate into an integrated plan); 4.3 Direct and Manage Project Work (lead and perform the planned work and implement approved changes); 4.4 Manage Project Knowledge (use existing and create new knowledge to achieve objectives and contribute to organisational learning); 4.5 Monitor and Control Project Work (track, review, report overall progress against plan objectives); 4.6 Perform Integrated Change Control (review all change requests, approve and manage changes to deliverables, OPAs, documents and the plan, communicate decisions); 4.7 Close Project or Phase (finalise all activities for project, phase or contract). Presented discretely but overlap in practice. Full ITTO lists recorded in docs/pmp-curriculum/ittos.json from Figure 4-1.

i-key-concepts.title: Key concepts, trends and tailoring for Integration Management; agile considerations
i-key-concepts.section: 4 key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile considerations
i-key-concepts.notes: Integration is specific to the PM: other areas may be handled by specialists, but accountability for integration cannot be delegated or transferred; the PM combines results from all areas and is ultimately responsible for the whole project. Projects are integrative (a contingency cost estimate integrates cost, schedule and risk processes) and links between Process Groups are iterative (planning hands executing a plan early and updates it as changes occur). Integration ensures alignment of deliverable dates, life cycle and benefits plan; provides the plan; creates and uses knowledge; manages performance and changes; makes integrated decisions on key changes; measures progress and acts; collects data, analyses it and communicates information; completes the work and formally closes phases, contracts and the project; manages phase transitions. Complexity and varied expectations demand more sophisticated integration. Trends: automated tools and PMIS; visual management tools; project knowledge management for a mobile workforce; expanding PM responsibilities (business case, benefits management, broader stakeholder engagement); hybrid methodologies (agile, business analysis for requirements, complexity tools, organisational change management). Tailoring: project life cycle, development life cycle (predictive/adaptive, incremental/iterative, hybrid), management approaches, knowledge management, change, governance (control boards, committees, reporting), lessons learned, benefits reporting timing. Agile: team members act as local domain experts and decide how plans and components integrate; PM's expectations unchanged but detailed product planning and delivery control is delegated to the team; PM builds collaborative decision-making and the ability to respond to change; generalising specialists help.
